title: T776 Form Canada
metaDescription: Learn how to fill out T776 form Canada step by step as a small landlord. Understand CRA deadlines, T776 line numbers, and avoid costly mistakes with our guide.
content:
As a Canadian landlord with 1-5 properties, understanding how to fill out T776 form Canada step by step is crucial for tax compliance. If you're confused or worried about this topic, you're not alone. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) requires landlords to report their rental income and expenses on the T776 form, which can be overwhelming. In this comprehensive guide, we'll walk you through every line of the T776 form, provide real-world examples, and help you avoid the most common mistakes Canadian landlords make.

## What Is the CRA T776 Form?

The T776 (Statement of Real Estate Rentals) is the official CRA form used to report rental income and expenses from real estate properties in Canada. Every landlord who earns rental income must file a T776 as part of their annual T1 General tax return — even if you operated at a loss or only rented part of the year.

The form captures your gross rental income, all eligible expenses, and the resulting net rental income (or loss), which flows directly into your tax return. The CRA uses this information to assess your tax liability and determine whether your rental activity qualifies as a business or property income.

**Who must file:** Any individual or corporation that earns rental income from real estate in Canada, including long-term rentals, short-term/vacation rentals (like Airbnb), basement suites, and rooms rented in your principal residence.

**When to file:** The T776 must be filed with your T1 General return by April 30th of each year. If you or your spouse/common-law partner are self-employed, the deadline extends to June 15th — but any balance owing is still due April 30th.

## T776 Line-by-Line Walkthrough

Understanding the T776 line numbers is the most important step to filing accurately. Here is a complete walkthrough of every section:

### Section A: Property Identification

**Line 1 — Type of property:** Select whether the property is a house, apartment, condominium, or other type. If you own multiple rental properties, you must file a separate T776 for each property or group properties of the same type together.

**Line 2 — Address of the property:** Enter the full street address of the rental property. This must match the address on your property tax assessment.

**Line 3 — Period during which you earned rental income:** Indicate the start and end dates of the rental period. If you rented the property for only part of the year (for example, if you converted a personal residence to a rental on July 1st), you would enter July 1st to December 31st.

### Section B: Income

**Line 800 — Gross rental income:** Report the total rent received or receivable during the calendar year. This includes:
- Base rent from tenants
- Parking fees charged separately
- Laundry income (if you operate coin laundry)
- Pet fees or other tenant-paid charges
- Any rent received in advance (accrual method)

**Example:** If you received $2,000/month in rent for 12 months plus $50/month for parking, your gross rental income would be $24,600 ($24,000 + $600).

**Important:** Report the full amount you collected, even if some months were paid late or a tenant owes you back rent. The CRA uses the cash method by default for small landlords.

### Section C: Expenses

This is where most landlords leave money on the table. Every eligible expense reduces your taxable rental income, so it's critical to claim everything you're entitled to.

**Line 8520 — Advertising:** Costs to find tenants, including online listing fees, newspaper ads, and "For Rent" signs. If you used a service like Kijiji or Rentals.ca, those fees are deductible here.

**Line 8590 — Insurance:** Property and liability insurance premiums for the rental property. If your insurance covers both the rental unit and your personal residence (for example, a duplex), you can only claim the rental portion.

**Line 8690 — Interest and bank charges:** Mortgage interest on money borrowed to acquire or improve the rental property. This is typically the largest deductible expense for Canadian landlords. You can only claim interest on the portion of the mortgage used for the rental property — not your personal residence.

**Example:** If your mortgage is $400,000 and you rent out half your duplex, you can claim interest on $200,000 of the mortgage balance.

**Line 8710 — Maintenance and repairs:** The cost of keeping the property in good condition, including painting, plumbing repairs, appliance repairs, and cleaning between tenants. These must be current expenses — if the work improves the property beyond its original condition (like a kitchen renovation), it may be classified as a capital expense and must be claimed as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) instead.

**Line 8810 — Management and administration fees:** Commissions paid to property managers, accounting fees for preparing your T776, and legal fees related to rental activities.

**Line 8690 — Office expenses:** Supplies, stationery, and other small office costs related to managing your rental property.

**Line 8860 — Professional fees:** Legal fees for tenant disputes, accounting fees for tax preparation related to rental income, and appraisal fees.

**Line 8871 — Property taxes:** Municipal property taxes paid for the rental property. If the property is partially personal-use, you can only claim the rental portion.

**Line 8990 — Salaries, wages, and benefits:** Wages paid to employees (not yourself) who work on the rental property, such as a part-time maintenance person or a live-in super.

**Line 9060 — Travel expenses:** Vehicle and travel expenses directly related to managing your rental property, including trips to collect rent, inspect the property, or meet with contractors. Keep a detailed log of each trip, including the date, destination, purpose, and distance.

**Line 9200 — Utilities:** Heat, electricity, water, and other utilities you pay for the rental unit. If the landlord pays utilities for a basement suite or apartment, these are fully deductible.

### Section D: Capital Cost Allowance (CCA)

**Line 9280 — CCA (depreciation):** You can claim CCA on the building portion of your rental property (not the land). Rental buildings fall under Class 1 (4% declining balance rate) or Class 3 (5% declining balance rate), depending on when the building was acquired.

**Important rules for CCA:**
- CCA is optional — you don't have to claim it every year
- You cannot create or increase a rental loss with CCA (the $2,500 rule for passive investors)
- The half-year rule applies in the year of acquisition (only 50% of net additions go into the CCA pool)
- If you sell the property, any recapture is taxed as income

**Example:** If you purchased a rental building for $300,000 (excluding land) in Class 1, your first-year CCA claim would be approximately $6,000 (4% × $300,000 × 50% for half-year rule = $6,000).

### Section E: Net Income Calculation

**Line 9369 — Total expenses:** Sum of all expenses from lines 8520 through 9280.

**Line 9946 — Net rental income (loss):** Subtract total expenses (line 9369) from gross rental income (line 800). This is the amount that flows into your T1 General return on line 12600.

## Special Scenarios

### Renting Part of Your Principal Residence

If you rent out a portion of your principal residence (such as a basement suite or a room), you must prorate expenses based on the square footage of the rental area relative to the total living space.

**Example:** If your home is 1,500 sq ft and you rent a 500 sq ft basement suite, you can claim 33% of shared expenses (mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, utilities) and 100% of expenses specific to the rental unit.

### Multiple Properties

If you own multiple rental properties, file a separate T776 for each property (or group properties of the same type). The CRA prefers individual property reporting for clarity, especially if properties are in different provinces or have different ownership structures.

### Short-Term Rentals (Airbnb)

Short-term rental income is reported the same way as long-term rental income on the T776. However, you may have additional obligations:
- Collect and remit GST/HST if your revenues exceed $30,000 over four consecutive quarters
- Collect municipal accommodation taxes in some cities
- Report income for each listing location separately

## CRA Deadlines and Penalties

The CRA deadline for filing the T776 form is April 30th of each year, unless you or your spouse/common-law partner are self-employed, in which case the deadline is June 15th. Failure to file on time can result in penalties, including a late-filing penalty of 5% of the balance owing, plus 1% per month, up to a maximum of 12 months.

**Example:** If you owe $10,000 in taxes and file 6 months late, you could be charged a penalty of $1,300 (5% × $10,000 = $500, plus 1% × $10,000 × 6 = $600, totaling $1,100 — though the exact calculation depends on your specific situation).

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

As a small landlord, it's easy to make mistakes when filling out the T776 form. Here are the most common errors we see:

### 1. Not Keeping Receipts
The CRA requires you to keep records for at least 6 years from the end of the tax year. Without receipts, you cannot prove your expenses in the event of an audit. Keep digital copies of all receipts, invoices, and bank statements related to your rental property.

### 2. Confusing Repairs with Capital Improvements
A repair (fixing something to its original condition) is a current expense. A capital improvement (upgrading beyond original condition) must be claimed as CCA. For example, repairing a broken window is a current expense; replacing all windows with energy-efficient models is a capital improvement.

### 3. Claiming Personal Expenses
Only expenses related to the rental use of the property are deductible. If you use part of the property for personal use, you must prorate expenses accordingly.

### 4. Failing to Report All Income
The CRA cross-references your T776 with other data sources, including tenant reports and provincial land registry records. If you fail to report rental income, you could face penalties, interest, and a full audit.

### 5. Not Filing a T776 at All
Some landlords don't realize they need to file a T776 if they had rental expenses but no net income (loss). Even if your expenses exceed your income, you must file — and the resulting loss can offset other income on your tax return.

## Record-Keeping Best Practices

The CRA requires accurate records for all rental activities. Follow these best practices:

- **Keep all receipts:** Store digital copies of every expense receipt for at least 6 years
- **Maintain a rental ledger:** Track income and expenses monthly, not just at tax time
- **Separate personal and rental finances:** Use a dedicated bank account for rental income and expenses
- **Document mileage:** Keep a log of all trips to the rental property, including date, purpose, and distance
- **Save lease agreements:** Keep copies of all signed tenancy agreements
- **Track capital improvements:** Maintain a separate list of capital expenditures for CCA calculations

## Key Takeaways

- File your T776 by April 30th each year (June 15th if self-employed)
- Report all rental income on line 800
- Claim every eligible expense on lines 8520–9200
- Understand the difference between current expenses and capital improvements
- Keep digital records for at least 6 years
- Consider CCA carefully — it's optional and has rules around rental losses
